1824.prule: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) in words of two or more syllables: disyllables (the great majority of simple roots) carry lexically specified final or penultimate stress (minimal pair /paka/ 'cará (fish)' vs /paka/ 'fishing net', differing only in stress); monosyllables are stressed.
1824.srule: Preliminary (Postigo 2014: 109, 'por vezes'): when a suffix draws primary stress to the word-final syllable, a secondary stress may remain on the syllable that carried primary stress in the base ([aˈnata] 'write' > [aˌnataˈpaj] 'is writing'); adjacent stresses are not permitted, so if that syllable abuts the new primary the secondary shifts one syllable further left ([tuˌlunaˈkuj] 'ear', *[tuluˌnaˈkuj]). No general rhythmic rule; fuller analysis of secondary stress deferred to future work; not marked in the orthography (p. 128).

It may be that this high pitch is a remnant of a recently lost lexical tone system.' (p.21); 'Kawe and Wauyai, currently do not feature lexical tone contrasts. These dialects have already lost their lexical tone system' (sec. 4.4.5).

tn.quote: Wauyai, like the other Maˈya dialects, has a system of lexical tone (contra Remijsen 2001a; 2001b, who analyses Wauyai as atonal). As in the other dialects, there are two tone specifications: Rise /σ¹²/ and High /σ³/. The tone system is culminative, in that only one syllable per word bears tone; in the vast majority of words, this is the final syllable. Words may also be toneless; toneless syllables are realised with low falling tone. ... Wauyai also has an orthogonal system of contrastive stress: in the majority of words, either the penultimate or final syllable of a word bears stress.

1826.prule: Penultimate, non-phonemic stress on the next-to-last vowel (syllables V/CV only; phonetically long vowels = two vowels, argued from stress placement). Stated by Mead (1998:16, 97) for all present-day Bungku-Tolaki languages, Wawonii explicitly among them, with one qualification: 'with suffixation usually precipitating stress movement' (stress normally shifts to the new penult of the suffixed word; no non-shifting suffix named). Mead 1999:101 (g) restates penultimate stress as the default reading of the word lists. Family-wide statement, not a Wawonii-specific description; no secondary stress, clitics or compounds discussed.

1827.prule: Primary accent on the final syllable of the prosodic word ('the rightmost syllable of the domain'; 'the most frequent pattern'), stated by Carvalho 2026:19-20 for the Amapari variety, which with the Ytuwasu/Upper Oyapock variety 'retain[s] the PTG pattern of ultimate accentuation'; forms with penultimate accent are 'usually analyzable' as carrying suffixes or enclitics that cannot bear accent, such as locative -pɛ ~ -mɛ ([ɛɾɛˈtãmɛ]), beside nouns with unaccented final -ã/-ɨ ([tapiˈʔiɾã], [ˈɛɾã], [ɨβɨˈtɨɾɨ]; §2.6.1 p.43); accentual retraction ([ˈakɛ], [ˈtata]; Jensen 1984:44) characterizes the Upper Jari variety specifically. Background from the previous edition: the sources reachable before 2026 disagreed, largely (not wholly) along dialect lines. Jensen 1999:133 STATES for 'Wayampi' (unqualified; her SIL fieldwork base was the Upper Jari variety per Carvalho 2023:3, though she cites Amapari data elsewhere in the chapter) stress on the penultimate syllable of unsuffixed or uncliticized stems, stem-final otherwise (the Tupi-Guarani default). Copin 2012 (Upper Oyapock variety, French Guiana) states no placement rule, but every stress-marked phonetic form (116/116, script count re-run by C; e.g. [paˈko], [tuˈle], [makuˈle], [jalaˈla], [soloˈlo], [a-poˈlaj]) is prosodic-word-final, including bare unsuffixed stems - incompatible with Jensen's penult statement for that variety. Carvalho 2023 (Amapari fieldwork) says accentual retraction, 'attributed to the Wajãpi language as whole', holds for Jari ([ˈjawa] < *jaˈwat) but NOT for Amapari ([jaˈwa], etymological placement; also [ˈaɾã] with unaccented final *-a), directly contradicting Jensen's unqualified claim for at least Amapari.

The 2011 MA (the only Glottolog reference) treats segmental phonology only; 'acento' appears twice in 239 pp., both incidental (o~u raising 'em sílabas não acentuadas'; an Apinajé comparison). 1829.heavy: Una sílaba pesada (P) contiene una vocal larga V1V1, un diptongo V1V2, o una vocal seguida de una consonante que cierra la sílaba VC.
1829.dflt: second syllable (whenever σ1 is light, regardless of later weights; third surface syllable if σ1 is extrametrical (C)Vʔ and the next is light)
1829.prule: Inspect the word-initial syllable: if heavy (long vowel, diphthong, or closed by a coda consonant) it is stressed; if light (single short vowel) the second syllable is stressed. A word-initial (C)Vʔ syllable (short vowel + glottal stop) is extrametrical and the count starts from the next syllable. Equivalent mora statement (Mosonyi & Jackson): stress the second mora, an initial saltillo-final mora not counting.
1829.srule: Not mentioned in Álvarez 2021 (§§1.1-1.7, pp.51-54: §1.7 locates only the sílaba tónica). Mosonyi & Jackson 1994-96 (pp.77-91) likewise give no secondary or rhythmic stress; they describe one pitch peak per lexeme ('el acento recae con carácter exclusivo sobre una sola mora', p.80).

1830.prule: Germanic (Dutch-type) system split by lexical stratum. (i) Native simplex words: stress on the first syllable (Sipma sec. 87); per Visser & Weening, native words normally contain only one full vowel, which attracts stress (schwa never stressed). (ii) Monomorphemic loanwords (the polysyllabic full-vowel vocabulary, borrowed via Dutch with the Dutch pattern): primary stress inside a right-edge three-syllable window, governed by weight-sensitive generalizations stated as tendencies - stress immediately precedes a schwa syllable; a closed penult with a full vowel blocks antepenult stress (aginda, fakansje); superheavy final syllables (A-class vowel + C, diphthong + C, B-class vowel + CC) and final diphthongs take final stress (aventoer, dokumint, batterij); a final closed syllable with a B-class vowel gives antepenult stress (albatros, karnaval; weak); a final open A-class-vowel syllable gives penult stress (aorta; but omega, brokkoly, orchidee). (iii) Complex words: morphology decides - verbal prefixes bi-, ge-, for-, ont-, to- unstressed (stress on stem-initial syllable), nominal prefixes ant-, oar-, on- stressed, suffixes -inne, -aezje, -es, -ier, -ij, -eare stress-bearing; compounds have no simple rule (mostly first element; some second; level stress in intensifying/comparative compounds).
1830.srule: Rhythmic and largely predictable from main stress (Visser & Weening 2015, stated as based mainly on the matching Dutch system): only in words of three or more syllables; syllables adjacent to the main stress are unstressed and the next ones out carry secondary stress (ˌre.sul.'taat, ˌle.di.'kant, ˌmak.kar.'roə.ni); the left edge is preferred (Hammock Principle), so 4-syllable words with final stress and 5-syllable words with penult stress have secondary stress on the first, not the second, syllable (ˌe:.ko:.no:.'mi, ˌɔr.ɡan.ni.'sa:s.jə), longer words combine both (ˌkom.pat.ti.ˌbi.li.'tɛit); schwa never stressed; not bound by the three-syllable window. In derived words Sipma 1913 marks half-stress on the stem after stressed prefixes ant-, oar-, on- and on the suffixes -dom, -heit, -skip, -achtich, -loas, -lei.

tn.quote: In tense a high-falling contour contrasts with a mid-rising contour. These contrastive contours are a characteristic of the morpheme and stretch over the 1 to 3 syllables of the morpheme. … The fall in the first contour is much more drastic than the rise in the second. The two intersecting systems of voice quality and pitch produce four contrasting patterns.

1841.heavy: Full vowels vs schwa: 'Stress skips over a non-final schwa and continues alternating from the syllable to the left'; additionally 'A sequence of two vowels may count as one mora in the stress rule'.
1841.dflt: With no non-final schwas: final syllable stressed and alternate syllables leftward (2σ σσ́ sikwán; 3σ σ́σσ́ páskihlá, kísikó; 4σ σσ́σσ́ awásɔnál).
1841.prule: Iterative alternating stress assigned right-to-left from the word end: the final syllable is stressed (including a final schwa), then every second syllable leftward; a non-final schwa (Warne's /e/) is skipped by the count and stress falls on the next syllable to its left (even if that is also a schwa); personal prefixes ne-, ke-, we- are never stressed; a VV sequence may count as one mora. Warne marks all stresses with the acute and does not distinguish primary from secondary stress.
1841.srule: Lesser (secondary) accents on every second syllable counting leftward from the primary-stressed final syllable, not counting syllables whose nucleus is schwa (e) (Day 1994 p. xi; = the non-final outputs of Warne's right-to-left alternating rule, e.g. áwasɔ́n, awásɔnál, páskihlá, nepáskenemén); an initial schwa syllable can carry a secondary accent (Day p. xii: bedegi, menahan); person prefixes ne-, ke-, we- never stressed (Warne p. 64).

1842.prule: Word accent falls on the first or second syllable of the word, i.e. inside the stem (stems are mono- or disyllabic and the language is exclusively suffixing; suffixes are unaccented). Default/majority: stem-final vowel (σ2 of a disyllabic stem); but σ1 for a lexically specified set of stems, with minimal pairs (kára-ni ‘fly’ vs kará-ni ‘write’, wéra-ni ‘go out’ vs werá-ni ‘cry’, píri-ni ‘approach’ vs pirí-ni ‘sing’). Position is therefore lexical within a left-edge two-syllable window; no weight conditioning; stated for Purepecha as a whole (eastern and western dialect areas) — accent placement is not among the east/west isoglosses Chamoreau lists (phonetic elisions, article order, comparative construction, OV order in Angahuan/San Lorenzo).
1842.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable counted rightward from the primary (σ1 or σ2), never on the word-final syllable: syllabic trochees built left-to-right from the lexical primary accent, e.g. ˈan.ʧi.ˌku.ɾi.ni 'trabajar', ku.ˈɾan.da.ˌɾa.za.ni̥ 'entendía', i.ˈʧux.pa.ˌta.ɾa.ˌŋas.ti.ˌksɨ.ŋḁ (San Luis Tsuren, NW Sierra). 1843.dq: WC does not have lexical stress; rather, WC word stress is predictable, always occurring on the final syllable. ... Postlexical prominence in WC is marked by both head marking and edge marking, because it uses both pitch accent (head marking) and IP and AP edge tones (edge marking).
1843.dloc: Ueki 2011 sec. 3.7.1 'Stress' p.51; ch.7 intro p.138; sec. 7.6 'Prosodic structure' p.163; sec. 6.2.2 pp.122-123 (trisyllable reduction). Friberg & Hor 1977 sec. 1 'Phonological word' p.18 and endnote 12.
1843.prule: Fixed word-final (iambic) stress: every phonological word ends in a heavily stressed main syllable; the optional presyllable is weakly stressed/reduced (vowel mostly schwa); in the small (<1% of lexicon) class of trisyllables the first syllable is weak, the medial syllable further reduced (often deleted), the final stressed. Weight/vowel length plays no role in placement. Acoustically (Ueki ch.6) final syllables have >2x the duration, greater intensity and pitch excursion than presyllables.
1843.srule: Disyllables (the canonical word) have one stress, on the final syllable; the presyllable is unstressed and reduced. In the small class of trisyllables (<1% of the lexicon) the first (pretonic) syllable is weakly stressed, the medial (atonic) syllable unstressed and further reduced (often deleted), the final syllable primary-stressed (Friberg & Hor 1977 p.18); Headley 1991 p.115 marks this as secondary stress on the first syllable in Kompong Thom Cham. No alternating rhythm; Ueki 2011 does not discuss secondary stress.

1843.exq_: Every phonological word ends with heavy stress. (Friberg & Hor 1977 p.18); WC word stress is predictable, always occurring on the final syllable. (Ueki 2011 p.163)
1843.tone: Not tonal. Western Cham has a two-way register (voice quality + pitch + vowel quality) contrast functioning at the phonological-word level, inherited from onset voicing as in Khmer (Friberg & Hor 1977; Ueki 2011 sec. 3.4); Ueki: 'EC is thought to have incipient tonal characteristics, whereas WC is thought to have phonemic voice quality distinctions.' Register is orthogonal to the fixed final stress. Postlexically Ueki finds pitch accents (on stressed syllables only) plus AP/IP boundary tones.

1844.prule: CONFLICT under one glottocode (Glottolog wich1263 'Vejoz' = ISO wlv, which carries the dialect 'Bermejo Vejoz' berm1242 and files Nercesian's Bermejo grammar as MED). (i) Tovar 1981 (informant Santos Aparicio, aiyu/Vejoz proper, Embarcación-Orán, Salta): accent is a property of the phrase, not the word; position set by phrase rhythm and focus; the same word is stressed on different syllables (wétes ~ wetés, Tagfwái ~ Tágfwaj); no word-stress rule. (ii) Nercesian 2011 (Bermejo/Teuco dialect, Abajeños, Formosa; instrumental, wordlists in isolation and connected speech): word-level, explicitly quantity-insensitive, iambs left-to-right, primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot of the phonological word = word-final primary stress in every monomorphemic base (ten.té, ʔi.nót, ʔa.tsì.n̥á, ʔis.tì.wín) and in affixed/cliticized PWords (la.pò.lé, n̩.yìs.tʰi.là.ʔám), with a listed set of morphological exceptions (extrametrical Type I locative/directional suffixes -> penultimate primary; noun-incorporation template). She reports Gerzenstein 2004 (Bermejo: last syllable, occasionally penult/antepenult) and Terraza 2009 (Rivadavia: nouns final, verbs less predictable) as concurring. Tovar's denial of a word domain is irreconcilable with Nercesian's explicit word-domain fixed-final analysis; they describe different sub-varieties (Nercesian, after Gerzenstein 2003, separates Bermejo from 'Salteño' = Güisnay+Vejoz) that the glottocode lumps.

In noun incorporation, secondary stress falls on the verbal root (primary on the first syllable of the incorporated noun). Tovar 1981 (Vejoz-proper leg) recognises no word stress and gives no secondary stress; he only reports Viñas Urquiza's attempt to mark 'un acento primario y otro secundario' (p. 172).

Perturbations: a non-/a/ vowel in a would-be unstressed position takes secondary stress (yépèn); about twenty forms carry secondary stress on second-syllable /a/ (pátàm); Class II/IV suffixes carry innate secondary stress (see morphology note).

evidence_works.work: McConnel 1945, Wikmunkan phonetics (Oceania 15(4): 353-375)
evidence_works.detail: Pre-SIL first-hand description from 'a post-field analysis of Wikmunkan texts recorded in 1934' and 'Nor has there since been an opportunity of checking the results of this analysis' (p.354); the texts were 'recorded at that time only as a means of obtaining direct information of cultural ideas', so the basis is post-field analysis of a text corpus, not elicitation. 'Stress' section pp.373-375: 'In words of two syllables stress falls on the first syllable' (p.373); 'In words of three syllables stress usually falls on the main syllable, which is usually the first' (p.373); 'In longer words the first syllable takes the strongest stress and the third syllable is weaker' (p.374), i.e. the record's 1 0 2 0 shape. Her further statements concern polymorphemic words and compounds: in a trisyllabic compound or a verb root with pronominal suffixes 'the main accent is directed towards the distinguishing element' (pp.373-374); four-syllable words built from two disyllables carry 'the main accent falling on the second qualifying word' (p.374); 'Where repetition of a stem occurs the accent falls on the last repeated syllable' (p.374). These match the record's treatment of non-initial primary stress as compounds/phrases and of suffix stress classes (Kilham 1977 sec 3.1.3, 3.1.6) and do not bear on the monomorphemic rule.

1848.prule: Word accent is a distinctive suprasegmental phoneme (lexically: Sua (woman's name) vs Suá (man's name); grammatically: lima 'hand' vs limá 'his/her hand', 3sg possessor/object marked by accent shift to the final syllable), confined to the last two syllables. Where no distinctive accent is present, position is predictable from the rhyme structure of penult and ultima: if penult and/or ultima is closed -> ULTIMA stressed (Anhang I no. 72 talŋa 'his/her ear' CVC.CV [taɫˈɴaʔ]; no. 73 vadaŋ 'sun' CV.CVC [ʋaˈɾaɴ]; no. 80 kainla 'later' CVV̯C.CV [qɐɪ̯n̪ˈɫaʔ]); if both open -> penult in the unmarked case (no. 70 dara 'blood' [ˈd̪aːɾɐʔ]; no. 77 vaina 'already' CVV̯.CV penult-stressed) vs ultima in the marked/distinctive case (no. 71 dará 'his/her blood', CVCV́). Realized mainly by lengthening of the stressed vowel and change of its quality.
1848.srule: Morphologically placed secondary accent only: roots (and their suffixed reduplications) always keep their accent; when suffixation establishes a new primary accent to the right (structurally required by a closed final/penult rhyme, or an inherently accented suffix), the root's original accent becomes a secondary accent (grave): moàge-da 'our liver', koàkoá 'go'; stems likewise keep a secondary accent under reduplication (ia-iáu). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress is described; a clitic group carries one accent.

vlen.q: Vowel length is also used to differentiate sounds in Cree: for instance, there is a difference between ota 'behind' and ōta 'here' -- where the macron, or bar, above the 'o' marks length. In Cree, therefore, o and ō are different phonemes.

tn.quote: Like other Cree dialects, Woods Cree stress is fixed and predictable, rather than lexically determined. ... Schmirler & Arnhold (2017) report that stress in Plains Cree primarily manifests through rises in pitch and intensity, but also report that these pitch contours are governed principally by a phrasal pitch accent system ... Although, impressionistically, Woods Cree stress also appears to primarily impact pitch and intensity, I have investigated this matter at only a very cursory level, and leave the nature of the acoustics of Woods Cree stress as an open question to future researchers.

1850.prule: Non-phonemic word stress (no minimal pairs). Basic/default stress is paroxytone (penultimate); stress tends to go to the syllable with greater moraic weight -- closed syllables and long-vowel syllables (diphthongs with variable effect) -- which accounts for most oxytone (final) stresses. Proparoxytone stress also attested (ex. 37).

tn.translation: Accent has been considered highly predictable by those who have treated Waunana phonology (Loewen 1954, Holmer 1963, Binder & Binder 1974, Sánchez & Castro 1977), although all except Holmer have held that there are exceptions that justify giving it phonemic status. … Consequently, it is considered that in Waunana a change took place that regularized the placement of the accent (which was originally free, as in Proto-Emberá) on the penultimate syllable.
